fields.raw_title: The Vaccine Paradox: Why High Coverage Still Hides Epidemics
raw_paragraphs: Global measles cases plummeted from nearly four million in 1980 to under two hundred thousand by the early 2020s. Yet, a sharp spike pushed reported infections back above half a million in 2024.

Nigeria stands out as an alarming outlier with 57% vaccination coverage and over sixty-five cases per million people. In contrast, Germany boasts near-universal protection at 96%, yet still recorded nearly seven thousand infections.
fields.moderated_title: Measles Trends and Vaccination Coverage Correlation
moderated_paragraphs: Global measles cases decreased from approximately 3.8 million in 1980 to roughly 200,000 by the early 2020s. However, reported infections increased to over 675,000 in 2024.
Nigeria reports 65.8 cases per million people with 57% vaccination coverage. In contrast, Germany recorded 7.6 cases per million despite having a 96% vaccination rate.

fields.human_text:
For two decades, measles looked like a problem the world was solving. Between 2000 and 2016, reported cases fell by more than half as first-dose vaccination climbed from 72% into the mid-80s. The trend line pointed in one direction.

Then it stopped. Coverage settled in the low-to-mid 80s and never reached the roughly 95% needed to hold the virus back. In 2019, before the pandemic disrupted reporting, cases climbed back above 860,000, the worst year in a generation.

The pattern is not mysterious. Measles is among the most contagious diseases we know, and it finds the gaps we leave. Where coverage holds, it retreats; where coverage slips, it returns. The data is less a warning than a reminder of how little margin there is.

fields.raw_title: The Mismatch: High Vaccines, Still Spreading
raw_paragraphs: In the last half-century, global vaccination coverage soared from just 16% in 1980 to 84% today. Yet measles cases have defied this progress, rebounding sharply in recent years despite high first-dose rates worldwide.
Nigeria illustrates a stark reality: with only 57% of children vaccinated and over 65 cases per million people, it dominates the global case count due to low herd immunity thresholds.
moderated_paragraphs: Over the last 40 years, global first-dose measles vaccine coverage increased from 16% in 1980 to approximately 84% today. While cases have fluctuated over time, recent data shows a rise in reported cases despite high vaccination rates in many regions.

Nigeria highlights the impact of lower coverage: with 57% of children vaccinated, it reports 65.8 cases per million people. In contrast, countries like India and Germany maintain higher coverage (over 96%) and report significantly lower incidence rates of 12.9 and 7.6 per million, respectively.

payload.title: The Mismatch: High Vaccines, Still Spreading
paragraphs: In the last half-century, global vaccination coverage soared from just 16% in 1980 to 84% today. Yet measles cases have defied this progress, rebounding sharply in recent years despite high first-dose rates worldwide.

payload.rationale: 'Stark reality' frames a specific country's data as universally alarming.

"defied this progress, rebounding sharply" and "stark reality" push mild dramatization above calibrated, while the framing of high coverage as a failed 'mismatch' and the omission of the ~5.7x drop in cases since 1980 leaves the tone bleaker than the data warrants.
